newsitem.title: USA: U.S. commission earnings may ratchet ECI higher.
newsitem.headline: U.S. commission earnings may ratchet ECI higher.

text.p: Despite heavy attention to the hourly earnings component of Friday's December nonfarm payrolls report, economists warned that a more important earnings reading could jolt the market later this month.
Even if Friday's report shows tame hourly earnings, a surprise could be lurking in the Employment Cost Index (ECI), to be released Jan 28, they said.
A sharp selloff in Treasuries could result, they said, if the ECI shows a dramatic rebound in sales commission earnings from weak third-quarter levels.
A less-than-expected 0.6 percent rise in third-quarter ECI sparked a bond market rally so sharp that yields on long-term Treasuries slid 15 basis points, economists at Smith Barney Inc noted.
Conversely, a strong ECI reading could spark a selloff by lending more credence to the growing notion that the U.S. economy saw strong growth in the fourth quarter of 1996.

The mild third-quarter ECI was largely the result of lower broker commission income on Wall Street as stock market losses chased away investors, William Sullivan, director of fixed-income research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc, explained.
"That obviously won't be the case in the fourth quarter," Sullivan said.
As a quarterly snapshot on earnings conditions, the ECI -- compiled by the Labor Department -- is considered more reliable and less subject to monthly swings in earnings data.

"It's certainly a better number than the hourlies, that's why it was created in 1980 or so," said David Monroe, chief U.S. economist with High Frequency Economics. "And it should show some heating up in the fourth quarter."

Steven Wieting, an associate economist at Smith Barney, noted that white collar earnings increased 3.6 percent in the third quarter of last year, but that excluding white collar sales occupations the gain in earnings was 3.8 percent.
Likewise, earnings in the goods sector rose 3.3 percent but excluding sales occupations 3.4 percent. The service sector rise was 3.3 percent, excluding sales 3.4 percent.
"So in every category year-over-year earnings increases were supressed when sales occupations were included," Wieting said.
He said his firm's preliminary estimates call for ECI to rise 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter, up from the third quarter gain of 0.6 percent.

But even with some heating up in the ECI, High Frequency Economics' Munro argued a fourth-quarter increase between 0.7 percent and 1.0 percent would be reasonable at a time when most corporations continue to reduce benefit costs.
Munro said if benefits savings were subtracted, wage growth still remained at about 2.0 percent, not enough to spur the Federal Reserve to tighten monetary policy.
"We know there's a lot happening to lighten up on benefits, so even a 0.8 percent fourth quarter reading comes out to about 3.25 percent on an annualized basis," Munro said.

On a broader note, Donald Ratajczak, director of the economic forecasting center at Georgia State University, expected the year-over-year ECI would increase to 3.3 percent from last year's 3.2 percent.

"The Fed is clearly concerned about wages but they're also looking at underlying factors," Ratajczak said. "We've had a surprising spurt in construction, but that won't last and you don't react to things that are going to go away."
